title: Howard Hyde's death caused by struggle with jail guards, inquiry report says
article: The head of an inquiry into the jail cell death of a mentally ill Nova Scotia man has rejected a medical examiner's conclusion that Howard Hyde died of excited delirium, finding instead the death was caused by a struggle with jail guards.

Anne Derrick, the provincial court judge who led the 11-month fatality inquiry, released a final report Wednesday that says the guards' restraint technique played a role in Hyde's accidental death on Nov. 22, 2007.

Derrick says Hyde, a 45-year-old musician diagnosed with schizophrenia in his 20s, was in the midst of a psychotic episode when he was forced to lie on his stomach with his hands behind his back, a position that may have interfered with his ability to breathe.

"The only useful approach is to understand that Mr. Hyde died because of physiological changes in his body brought on by an intense struggle involving restraint," Derrick wrote. "He did not die because he was mentally ill."

Kevin MacDonald, a lawyer representing the Hyde family, had argued that the cause of death was the restraint method, which left the overweight man face down, his left ankle locked behind his right knee.

"This whole notion of excited delirium tends to place blame on the victim," MacDonald said in an interview Wednesday. "It did that in this case with Mr. Hyde. Furthermore, we're not convinced that it exists as an entity."
Derrick said she agreed with one expert witness who testified that citing excited delirium as a cause of death resulted in Hyde being "identified as the culprit."
The inquiry heard from other witnesses who said the condition is characterized by increased strength, paranoia and suddenly violent behaviour marked by profuse sweating and an elevated heart rate.
Hyde demonstrated most of the traits in the hours before he died, the inquiry heard.
The causes of excited delirium, according to one expert, may include schizophrenia and other psychiatric illnesses, drug intoxication, alcohol withdrawal and heat stroke.
However, Dr. Joseph Noone, an expert on the clinical aspects of violent behaviour, told the inquiry the term is "unsatisfactory from a psychiatry point of view."
An independent report commissioned by the RCMP also criticized the use of the term.

The report, ordered after Polish immigrant Robert Dziekanski died after he was Tasered by a Mountie at Vancouver International Airport, said the condition is sometimes used as an excuse to justify firing stun guns.

Hyde's story attracted national attention because he had been Tasered up to five times by Halifax police about 30 hours before he died. But Derrick's 460-page report clearly states the repeated Tasering did not cause Hyde's death.
Still, the judge recommended that conducted energy weapons (CEWs) should not be used to immobilize emotionally disturbed people unless crisis intervention techniques have failed.

"Use of the CEW on Mr. Hyde worsened the situation," Derrick wrote, repeatedly calling attention to the fact that police, health and corrections staff testified they had received little training on how to deal with mentally ill people.
During the hearings, which wrapped up in June, the Halifax Regional Police argued that its officers are trained not to stun anyone until de-escalation techniques have been tried.
But Derrick rejected this argument, saying police policy and the province's standards make no mention of this requirement.

As well, her report recommends the provincial Justice Department overhaul the manual it uses for stun gun training, saying it should reduce if not eliminate content from Taser International, a stun gun manufacturer.
Many of Derrick's 80 recommendations call for improved training, more funding for mental health services and better co-ordination and communication between justice and health officials.
Derrick also rejected the medical examiner's conclusion that Hyde's death was "due to schizophrenia."
"Schizophrenia would not have killed him," she wrote. "It did make him fearful, anxious and delusional but it is completely unhelpful to link his death to his diagnosis of schizophrenia."
She said Dr. Matthew Bowes's decision to describe the underlying cause of death as schizophrenia only stigmatized Hyde's mental illness.
"Such a characterization suggests ... that Mr. Hyde's death was somehow inevitable, that he died because he was 'a schizophrenic;' that 'normal' people would not die in the same circumstances."
Joanna Blair, Hyde's sister, said she was relieved by the judge's decision to challenge the official cause of death.
"She got rid of what I consider the mythical terms of excited delirium," Blair said in an interview from her home in Clark's Harbour, N.S.
"She also said in the report that to say my brother died of schizophrenia was to stigmatize him as a person suffering from a mental illness. To say that it was a cause of death was ridiculous."

Stephen Ayer, executive director of the Schizophrenia Society of Nova Scotia, said he was thrilled with the report, saying his group supports Derrick's call for an increase in funding for mental health services and the appointment of a provincial director of mental health strategy.
The director would be responsible for implementing the recommendations and overseeing the proposed strategy.
"I couldn't have written better recommendations myself," Ayer said.

Ross Landry, Nova's Scotia's justice minister, issued a statement Wednesday saying the "tragic incident" at the province's largest jail will be a catalyst for "real and positive change in the system."
"I wish to convey my sympathy to the family and assure them that we will carefully consider the recommendations contained in this report," Landry said.
During the inquiry, Derrick learned Hyde had long taken medication to cope with schizophrenia.
On the night of Nov. 21, 2007, his common-law wife, Karen Ellet, accused him of assaulting her, telling police he had not been taking his medications for some time.
When he was arrested near the couple's apartment, Hyde was wearing only a pair of shorts, even though the temperature was around the freezing mark.
The inquiry also heard that Ellet told police her husband needed psychiatric treatment. Despite her request, Hyde was never given the help he needed.
The two police officers who arrested Hyde failed to pass along information about his mental state to the booking officers at the Halifax police station, Derrick found.
Once inside police headquarters, Hyde tried to flee when an officer tried to cut a knot on the string holding up his shorts, saying, "We'll have to cut one of those balls off."
"These words lit the fuse for the explosive events that followed," Derrick wrote.

During the ensuing struggle, Hyde was hit with the stun gun several times, and police restrained him by placing him on his stomach, cuffing his hands behind his back and pushing his lower legs toward his back.
"Neither the video nor the audio evidence from the booking hallway indicate that Mr. Hyde was being combative," Derrick wrote.
At one point, Hyde fell unconscious. One of the officers at the scene revived him using mouth-to-mouth resuscitation.

Hyde was later taken to hospital where he was given an anti-psychotic medication, but he was released several hours later with a doctor's note scrawled on a health information transfer form, saying he should be returned to the emergency ward if a court failed to grant him a psychiatric assessment.
Derrick found that the doctor who released Hyde did so because she "felt a sense of urgency" after talking to an officer who said Hyde needed to appear before a judge.
As well, the doctor believed it was likely Hyde would receive a court-ordered psychiatric assessment.
But the doctor's instructions were never conveyed to Crown and defence lawyers because of privacy concerns. The judge hearing the case did not order an assessment.
Instead, Hyde was sent to the Central Nova Scotia Correctional Facility in suburban Dartmouth.
The next morning, guards wrestled him to the ground after he refused to walk down a hallway, screaming that he was afraid of the "demons'' at the other end.
Derrick's report says the guards should have used crisis intervention techniques to calm Hyde's fears, but she noted that none of the officers involved had any training in mental health issues.
The struggle inside a holding cell lasted about two and a half minutes before Hyde went limp and stopped breathing.
